content: Carbonyl reductase 1 (CBR1) is an enzyme encoded by the CBR1 gene in humans. This enzyme is a member of the short-chain dehydrogenases/reductases (SDR) family, which are NADPH-dependent oxidoreductases. These enzymes exhibit broad substrate specificity for carbonyl compounds, including quinones, prostaglandins, and various xenobiotics. Alternative splicing of the CBR1 gene has been observed, resulting in transcript variants. Function CBR1 is one of several monomeric, NADPH-dependent oxidoreductases with broad specificity for carbonyl compounds. It is widely distributed across human tissues. Another carbonyl reductase gene, CBR3, is located near CBR1 on chromosome 21q. CBR1 metabolizes numerous toxic environmental quinones and pharmacologically relevant substrates, such as the anticancer drug doxorubicin. Research has demonstrated that CBR1 plays a protective role in oxidative stress, neurodegeneration, and apoptosis. Additionally, CBR1 inactivates lipid aldehydes during oxidative stress in cells, suggesting its potential role in protecting against cellular damage caused by oxidative stress. Polymorphisms Two non-synonymous polymorphisms in the CBR1 gene have been identified. The CBR1 V88I polymorphism results in a valine-to-isoleucine substitution at position 88 of the amino acid chain. In vitro studies using recombinant proteins indicate that the CBR1 V88 isoform exhibits a higher Vmax for substrates such as menadione (vitamin K3) and daunorubicin. Furthermore, studies in human liver cytosols have shown that an untranslated polymorphism in the 3' UTR region of the CBR1 gene (rs9024) is associated with increased levels of the cardiotoxic metabolite doxorubicinol. Protein The CBR1 enzyme consists of 277 amino acid residues and is widely expressed in human tissues, including the liver, epidermis, stomach, small intestine, kidney, neuronal cells, and smooth muscle fibers. Its preferred substrates are quinones, such as ubiquinone-1 and tocopherol quinone (vitamin E). Ubiquinones (coenzyme Q) are integral components of the respiratory chain, while tocopherol quinone protects biological membrane lipids from lipid peroxidation. These findings suggest that CBR1 may play a critical role as an oxidation-reduction catalyst in various biological processes. Clinical Significance CBR1 has been implicated in tumor progression. Reduced expression of CBR1 has been associated with poor prognosis in uterine endometrial cancer and uterine cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Previous studies have also linked decreased CBR1 expression to lymph node metastasis and poor prognosis in ovarian cancer. Induction of CBR1 expression in ovarian tumors has been shown to result in spontaneous tumor size reduction. Recent research indicates that CBR1 attenuates apoptosis and promotes cell survival in pancreatic β-cell lines under glucotoxic and glucolipotoxic conditions by reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Data suggest that CBR1 expression and enzyme activity are decreased in pancreatic islets isolated from db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes. These findings imply that CBR1 may protect pancreatic β-cells from oxidative stress under glucotoxic or glucolipotoxic conditions, and its reduced expression or activity may contribute to β-cell dysfunction in db/db mice or human type 2 diabetes. Additionally, CBR1 may play a critical role in prostaglandin F2α (PGF2α) synthesis in human amnion fibroblasts. Cortisol promotes the conversion of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) into PGF2α via glucocorticoid receptor (GR)-mediated induction of CBR1 in human amnion fibroblasts. This stimulatory effect of cortisol on CBR1 expression may partially explain the concurrent increases in cortisol and PGF2α in human amnion tissue during labor. These findings may also account for the increased production of PGF2α in fetal membranes prior to the onset of labor. Interactions CBR1 has been shown to interact with cortisol, the C2 domain, and flavonoids.
